category: Phrasal verbs on regular bases: G-L

entries.meaning: To get closer to someone or something ahead of you. ---
examples: That blue car has been gaining on us since the last exit.
She gained on the leader with every lap.
By mile ten he had gained on the whole front pack.
entries.separable: inseparable — the object follows on: gaining on us, never ✗ gain us on.
entries.forms: gain on · gained on · gained on

entries.meaning: To join with others against one person. ---
examples: Don't all gang up on me at once.
The other kids ganged up on him at recess.
Three networks are ganging up on the same story.
entries.русский: ополчаться, ополчиться (на кого-л.); наваливаться всем вместе
entries.separable: inseparable — the target comes after on: they ganged up on him, never ✗ they ganged him up on. Without a target it stands alone: they all ganged up.
entries.forms: gang up on · ganged up on · ganged up on
entries.third person: gangs up on · -ing form: ganging up on

entries.meaning: To fill a vehicle's tank with gasoline. ---
examples: I need to gas up before we get on the highway.
He gassed up the truck at the station on Route 9.
We're gassing up and then heading straight out.
entries.separable: separable — gas up the car or gas the car up, and with a pronoun it must split: gas it up. Just as often there is no object at all: we stopped to gas up.
entries.forms: gas up · gassed up · gassed up
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (gas up the truck), intransitive (stop and gas up)

entries.meaning: To collect scattered things quickly into one armful or pile. ---
examples: Gather up your things — the bus leaves in five minutes.
She gathered up the papers that had blown off the desk.
He was gathering the kids' shoes up by the door.
entries.separable: separable — gather up the toys, gather the toys up, and with a pronoun gather them up.
entries.forms: gather up · gathered up · gathered up

entries.meaning: To design or aim something at a particular group or purpose. ---
examples: They geared the whole class toward absolute beginners.
These ads are geared toward buyers under thirty.
We're gearing the campaign toward first-time voters.
entries.русский: ориентировать, сориентировать (на кого-л.); рассчитывать (на определённую публику)
entries.separable: the object always sits between the two parts — gear the class toward beginners, gear it toward beginners; ✗ gear toward beginners the class. Learners meet it most often in the passive: the course is geared toward beginners.
entries.forms: gear toward · geared toward · geared toward

entries.meaning: To get ready for something big or demanding that is coming. ---
examples: Stores gear up for the holidays right after Halloween.
The team geared up for a long playoff run.
We've been gearing up for this inspection all month.
entries.separable: usually no object — the thing you are getting ready for arrives through for: gear up for the season. When it does take an object it separates: gear the plant up for production, gear it up.
entries.forms: gear up · geared up · geared up
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (gear up for the holidays), transitive (gear the factory up)

entries.meaning: To read something quickly without studying it. ---
examples: Could you glance over this email before I send it?
She glanced over the menu and ordered the usual.
He's glancing over the numbers now and will call back.
entries.separable: inseparable — glance over the contract, never ✗ glance the contract over. (The separable one is look it over.)
entries.forms: glance over · glanced over · glanced over

entries.meaning: To look quickly through the pages of something, stopping nowhere long. ---
examples: I glanced through the report on the plane.
He glances through the paper while the coffee brews.
She was glancing through a magazine in the waiting room.
entries.separable: inseparable — glance through the report, never ✗ glance the report through.
entries.forms: glance through · glanced through · glanced through

entries.meaning: Of the eyes, to lose focus because the person has stopped taking anything in. ---
examples: His eyes glazed over halfway through the presentation.
Mention the tax code and everybody glazes over.
I could see the students glazing over, so I stopped.
entries.separable: no object — intransitive. The subject is the eyes, or the person behind them: his eyes glazed over, the whole room glazed over.
entries.forms: glaze over · glazed over · glazed over

entries.meaning: To mention something so briefly that its worst or hardest parts get no attention. ---
examples: The report glosses over the safety violations.
He glossed over the part where he lost the money.
She's been glossing over how hard that first year was.
entries.separable: inseparable — gloss over the problem, never ✗ gloss the problem over.
entries.forms: gloss over · glossed over · glossed over

entries.meaning: Of a worry, doubt, or guilt, to keep troubling someone for a long time. ---
examples: The mistake gnawed at her for months.
Something about his story keeps gnawing at me.
Guilt had been gnawing at him since March.
entries.separable: inseparable — the doubt gnawed at her, never ✗ gnawed her at. Often stretched for emphasis: gnaw away at.
entries.forms: gnaw at · gnawed at · gnawed at

entries.meaning: To swallow food quickly, almost without chewing. ---
examples: He gobbled down a sandwich and ran for the bus.
Don't gobble your dinner down like that.
They were gobbling down pancakes when I got there.
entries.separable: separable — gobble down breakfast, gobble your dinner down, gobble it down.
entries.forms: gobble down · gobbled down · gobbled down

entries.meaning: To buy up, take over, or use up something completely and fast. ---
examples: A bigger chain gobbled up the family stores one by one.
Rent gobbles up half her paycheck.
Developers are gobbling up the farmland east of town.
entries.separable: separable — gobble up the competition, gobble them up.
entries.forms: gobble up · gobbled up · gobbled up

entries.meaning: To eat something very fast and finish all of it. ---
examples: The kids gobbled up every last cookie.
He gobbles up whatever's left in the pan.
She's gobbling it up like she hasn't eaten in days.
entries.separable: separable — gobble up the last slice, gobble the last slice up, gobble it up.
entries.forms: gobble up · gobbled up · gobbled up

entries.meaning: To play and act silly instead of being serious. ---
examples: Quit goofing around and finish your homework.
We goofed around in the parking lot for an hour.
He goofs around in class and then wonders why he's failing.
entries.separable: no object — intransitive: quit goofing around. A companion arrives through with: goofing around with his cousins.
entries.forms: goof around · goofed around · goofed around

entries.meaning: To avoid the work you are supposed to be doing and waste time instead. ---
examples: He goofs off all afternoon and then stays late to catch up.
They goofed off the entire week the boss was away.
I've been goofing off instead of studying for the test.
entries.separable: no object — intransitive: he goofs off all day.
entries.forms: goof off · goofed off · goofed off

entries.meaning: To make a careless mistake, or to spoil something by making one. ---
examples: Sorry — I goofed up the order.
Everybody goofs up the first few times.
He keeps goofing up the easy ones and getting the hard ones right.
entries.separable: separable when there is an object — goof up the order, goof the order up, goof it up. Very often used with no object at all: I goofed up.
entries.forms: goof up · goofed up · goofed up
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (goof up the order), intransitive (sorry, I goofed up)

entries.meaning: To struggle hard to understand or deal with something difficult. ---
examples: The city is still grappling with its housing shortage.
She grappled with the decision for weeks.
We have grappled with this same question all year.
entries.separable: inseparable — grapple with the problem, never ✗ grapple the problem with.
entries.forms: grapple with · grappled with · grappled with

entries.meaning: To irritate someone steadily, a little more with every repetition. ---
examples: His laugh really grates on me.
The music grated on my nerves after the first hour.
Her constant corrections were grating on everyone at the table.
entries.separable: inseparable — it grates on me, never ✗ it grates me on. Often with nerves: grate on my nerves.
entries.forms: grate on · grated on · grated on

entries.meaning: To be drawn to a person, place, or kind of thing again and again. ---
examples: New students gravitate toward the loudest table in the room.
He gravitated toward jobs where nobody looked over his shoulder.
Buyers have been gravitating toward smaller cars all year.
entries.separable: inseparable — gravitate toward the back row, never ✗ gravitate the back row toward.
entries.forms: gravitate toward · gravitated toward · gravitated toward

entries.meaning: To disgust someone. ---
examples: That story totally grossed me out.
He grosses out his little sister on purpose.
The smell in the fridge was grossing everybody out.
entries.русский: вызывать отвращение, вызвать отвращение; противно кому-л.
entries.separable: separable — gross out the whole table or gross the whole table out, and with a pronoun it must split: it grossed me out, never ✗ it grossed out me.
entries.forms: gross out · grossed out · grossed out

entries.meaning: To act in advance so that something bad does not happen. ---
examples: Wash your hands to guard against infection.
The rule was written to guard against exactly this situation.
We're guarding against a repeat of last winter.
entries.русский: остерегаться, остеречься; принимать меры против, предотвращать
entries.separable: inseparable — guard against infection, never ✗ guard infection against.
entries.forms: guard against · guarded against · guarded against

entries.meaning: To swallow a drink or food quickly, in big mouthfuls. ---
examples: He gulped down a glass of water and kept running.
She gulps her coffee down on the way out the door.
They were gulping down soda between innings.
entries.separable: separable — gulp down the medicine, gulp your coffee down, gulp it down.
entries.forms: gulp down · gulped down · gulped down

entries.meaning: To clog something with something sticky, or to make a smooth process stop running. ---
examples: Sap had gummed up the saw blade.
One missing signature can gum up the whole process.
You're gumming up the works with all these extra forms.
entries.русский: забивать, забить (механизм); засорять, засорить; портить дело
entries.separable: separable — gum up the works, gum the machine up, gum it up. Common in the passive: the printer got gummed up.
entries.forms: gum up · gummed up · gummed up

entries.meaning: To shoot someone, usually killing them, when they cannot defend themselves. ---
examples: Two officers were gunned down in the street.
The robber gunned down a guard and ran.
In the opening scene he guns down a witness in broad daylight.
entries.separable: separable — gun down the suspect, gun him down. Most often heard in the passive: he was gunned down.
entries.forms: gun down · gunned down · gunned down

entries.meaning: To be looking for a chance to attack, blame, or get rid of a particular person. ---
examples: The new boss has been gunning for him since day one.
Reporters gunned for the mayor after the memo leaked.
Watch what you say in there — they're gunning for you.
entries.русский: ополчиться (на кого-л.); точить зуб, охотиться за кем-л.
entries.separable: inseparable — gunning for him, never ✗ gun him for.
entries.forms: gun for · gunned for · gunned for

entries.meaning: To be openly and hard at work trying to get something. ---
examples: She's gunning for the manager's job and everybody knows it.
He gunned for a starting spot all season.
Both teams are gunning for first place this weekend.
entries.separable: inseparable — gunning for the top job, never ✗ gun the job for.
entries.forms: gun for · gunned for · gunned for

entries.meaning: To praise someone or something in an excited, exaggerated way. ---
examples: Everyone gushed over the baby for twenty minutes.
She gushes over every picture he posts.
They were still gushing over the new kitchen when we left.
entries.separable: inseparable — gush over the baby, never ✗ gush the baby over. Gush about works the same way.
entries.forms: gush over · gushed over · gushed over

entries.meaning: To break into a computer system without permission. ---
examples: Someone hacked into the district's grading system.
Thieves are hacking into accounts with passwords stolen years ago.
He only hacks into systems he is paid to test.
entries.separable: inseparable — the system follows the whole phrase: hacked into the server, never ✗ hacked the server into.
entries.forms: hack into · hacked into · hacked into

entries.meaning: To come originally from a particular place. ---
examples: Both finalists hail from small towns in Iowa.
Her grandparents hailed from a village outside Naples.
The band, hailing from Detroit, sold out the show in an hour.
entries.separable: inseparable — the place always follows the whole phrase: hails from Ohio, never ✗ hails Ohio from.
entries.forms: hail from · hailed from · hailed from
entries.transitivity: transitive — always with a place after from

entries.meaning: To repeat a point forcefully until everyone understands it. ---
examples: The coach hammered home the same lesson at every practice.
She hammers the point home with one number: forty percent.
The campaign is hammering home a single slogan.
entries.separable: separable — hammer home the point or hammer the point home; with a pronoun it must split: hammer it home.
entries.forms: hammer home · hammered home · hammered home

entries.meaning: To reach an agreement or a plan after long, difficult discussion. ---
examples: The two sides hammered out a contract at four in the morning.
We still need to hammer out who pays for shipping.
They have been hammering out the details all week.
entries.separable: separable — hammer out a deal and hammer the deal out are both fine; with a pronoun it must split: hammer it out, never ✗ hammer out it.
entries.forms: hammer out · hammered out · hammered out

entries.meaning: To announce an official decision or sentence, as a court does. ---
examples: The Supreme Court handed down its decision on Thursday.
No one knows when the judge will hand down a sentence.
The panel has handed down tougher penalties since the rule changed.
entries.separable: separable in form — hand the sentence down — but in this legal sense it is usually left whole: hand down a ruling; with a pronoun it splits: hand it down.
entries.forms: hand down · handed down · handed down

entries.meaning: To pass something to a younger generation. ---
examples: The watch was handed down from his grandfather.
She hands down every winter coat to her younger sister.
Families here have been handing down the same recipes for a century.
entries.separable: separable — hand down a name, hand the recipe down; with a pronoun it must split: hand it down. Very often passive: handed down from her grandmother.
entries.forms: hand down · handed down · handed down

entries.meaning: To give a piece of work or a formal document to someone in authority. ---
examples: Hand in your tests when the bell rings.
He handed in his resignation on Monday.
She has already handed her application in.
entries.separable: separable — hand in your homework and hand your homework in are both fine; with a pronoun it must split: hand it in, never ✗ hand in it.
entries.forms: hand in · handed in · handed in

entries.meaning: To admit that someone deserves credit for something. ---
examples: You have to hand it to her — she never misses a deadline.
I've got to hand it to the kid; that was a great catch.
Even his critics handed it to him after the speech.
entries.separable: fixed — it never changes and never moves, and the person follows to: you have to hand it to her, never ✗ hand her it.
entries.forms: hand it to · handed it to · handed it to
entries.third person: hands it to · -ing form: handing it to
entries.transitivity: transitive — with the fixed object it

entries.meaning: To pass a task, a duty, or the ball to someone else. ---
examples: I'm handing off the account to Marcus on Friday.
The quarterback handed the ball off and got flattened.
Once the code is tested, it gets handed off to support.
entries.separable: separable — hand off the project, hand the project off; with a pronoun it must split: hand it off.
entries.forms: hand off · handed off · handed off

entries.meaning: To give something to each person in a group. ---
examples: Volunteers handed out bottled water at every mile.
Could you hand out these worksheets?
They were handing free samples out by the entrance.
entries.separable: separable — hand out the papers, hand the papers out; with a pronoun it must split: hand them out.
entries.forms: hand out · handed out · handed out

entries.meaning: To give something or someone to another person, usually because you have no choice. ---
examples: The robber told him to hand over his wallet.
She handed over the keys and called a cab.
Power was peacefully handed over in January.
entries.separable: separable — hand over the keys, hand the keys over; with a pronoun it must split: hand them over.
entries.forms: hand over · handed over · handed over

entries.meaning: To keep talking about the same complaint until it annoys people. ---
examples: He harps on my spending every time we go out.
She harped on the mistake for weeks.
Quit harping on the past.
entries.русский: твердить одно и то же, зудеть; долдонить
entries.separable: inseparable — the topic follows the whole phrase: harp on the same thing, never ✗ harp the same thing on.
entries.forms: harp on · harped on · harped on
entries.transitivity: transitive — always with on before the topic

entries.meaning: To talk something through at length until the details are settled. ---
examples: Let's hash out the schedule over lunch.
They hashed out their differences in the parking lot.
We're still hashing out who drives.
entries.русский: обсуждать, обсудить во всех деталях; утрясать, утрясти
entries.separable: separable — hash out the details, hash the details out; with a pronoun it must split: hash it out.
entries.forms: hash out · hashed out · hashed out

entries.meaning: To start traveling back toward the place you came from. ---
examples: We should head back before it gets dark.
They headed back to the campsite at sunset.
I'm heading back on the six o'clock train.
entries.separable: n/a — intransitive, so nothing can come between the parts; a destination takes to: head back to the hotel.
entries.forms: head back · headed back · headed back

entries.meaning: To be on course for a particular result, usually a bad one. ---
examples: The talks are heading for collapse.
We were headed for a shutdown until the last-minute deal.
Analysts say the economy could head for a slowdown next year.
entries.русский: двигаться к, идти к; неминуемо приближаться (к чему-то плохому)
entries.separable: inseparable — the outcome follows for: heading for trouble, never ✗ heading trouble for. Most often in the form be headed for.
entries.forms: head for · headed for · headed for
entries.transitivity: transitive — always with for before the outcome

entries.meaning: To get in front of someone in order to stop them from going where they were going. ---
examples: Two deputies headed off the truck at the county line.
If we cut across the field, we can head them off.
She was headed off by reporters before she reached her car.
entries.русский: перехватывать, перехватить; преграждать путь, преградить путь
entries.separable: separable — head off the runner, head the runner off; with a pronoun it must split: head him off.
entries.forms: head off · headed off · headed off

entries.meaning: To stop something bad from happening by acting before it does. ---
examples: The company raised wages to head off a strike.
A quick apology headed off a much bigger fight.
They're heading off complaints by refunding everyone.
entries.separable: separable — head off a strike, head the problem off; with a pronoun it must split: head it off.
entries.forms: head off · headed off · headed off

entries.meaning: To leave a place and set off somewhere. ---
examples: We're heading out at six to beat the traffic.
He headed out without saying goodbye.
Head out early if you want a parking spot.
entries.separable: n/a — intransitive, so nothing splits it; a destination takes for or to: head out for the lake.
entries.forms: head out · headed out · headed out

entries.meaning: To be in charge of a group, a team, or a project. ---
examples: She heads up the marketing team.
He headed up the investigation for two years.
A former teacher is heading up the new program.
entries.separable: separable in form — head the committee up is possible — but it is nearly always left whole: head up the committee. With a pronoun it does split: she heads it up.
entries.forms: head up · headed up · headed up

entries.meaning: To get completely better, of a wound or an injury. ---
examples: The cut healed up in a week.
Give it time and the blister will heal up on its own.
His shoulder is finally healing up.
entries.separable: n/a — intransitive here; the wound is the subject, not an object: the burn is healing up.
entries.forms: heal up · healed up · healed up

entries.meaning: To become more intense, more exciting, or more hostile. ---
examples: The race heated up after the second debate.
Things are heating up between the two companies.
Competition heats up every year around the holidays.
entries.separable: n/a in this sense — it takes no object: the race heated up.
entries.forms: heat up · heated up · heated up

entries.meaning: To make something warm again, or to become warm. ---
examples: I'll heat up the leftovers.
She heated the sauce up while the pasta boiled.
The oven is still heating up.
entries.separable: separable — heat up the soup, heat the soup up; with a pronoun it must split: heat it up, never ✗ heat up it.
entries.forms: heat up · heated up · heated up
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (heat up the leftovers), intransitive (the oven heats up fast)

entries.meaning: To give someone help, especially with work, money, or a favor. ---
examples: Could you help me out with the dishes?
His parents helped him out with the down payment.
She has been helping out at the food bank since March.
entries.separable: separable — help out a friend or help your sister out; with a pronoun it must split: help me out, never ✗ help out me.
entries.forms: help out · helped out · helped out
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (help a neighbor out), intransitive (she helps out on weekends)

entries.meaning: To take as much of something as you want without waiting to be served. ---
examples: Help yourself to whatever's in the fridge.
He helped himself to three slices before anyone sat down.
Guests were helping themselves to the buffet.
entries.русский: угощаться, угоститься; брать самому, взять самому
entries.separable: fixed — the reflexive pronoun matches the subject (help myself / yourself / themselves to), and the thing always follows to.
entries.forms: help yourself to · helped yourself to · helped yourself to
entries.third person: helps yourself to · -ing form: helping yourself to
entries.transitivity: transitive — with a reflexive pronoun and to

entries.meaning: To surround someone or something so closely that movement or choice is limited. ---
examples: Mountains hem in the valley on three sides.
We were hemmed in by traffic for an hour.
New rules are hemming in small landlords.
entries.separable: separable — hem in the valley, hem the horses in; with a pronoun it must split: hem them in. Usually passive: hemmed in by rules.
entries.forms: hem in · hemmed in · hemmed in

entries.meaning: To attach a trailer or an animal to whatever will pull it. ---
examples: He hitched up the camper before sunrise.
We hitch the boat up every Friday in the summer.
They were hitching up the horses when the rain started.
entries.separable: separable — hitch up the trailer, hitch the trailer up; with a pronoun it must split: hitch it up.
entries.forms: hitch up · hitched up · hitched up

entries.meaning: To shut yourself away somewhere for a while, hiding or avoiding people. ---
examples: The suspect holed up in a cabin for three days.
I'm going to hole up at home and finish the draft.
They have been holed up in the office since Monday.
entries.separable: n/a — intransitive, so nothing splits it; the place takes in: hole up in a motel.
entries.forms: hole up · holed up · holed up

entries.meaning: To weaken something from the inside until little of substance is left. ---
examples: Decades of layoffs hollowed out the town.
Automation is hollowing out middle-income jobs.
The agency has been hollowed out by budget cuts.
entries.separable: separable — hollow out the middle class, hollow the town out; with a pronoun it must split: hollow it out. Often passive: hollowed out by cuts.
entries.forms: hollow out · hollowed out · hollowed out

entries.meaning: To move or focus closely toward one target or one detail. ---
examples: Investigators homed in on a single email.
The camera homes in on one face in the crowd.
She's homing in on the cause of the bug.
entries.русский: нацеливаться на, нацелиться на; сосредоточиваться на, сосредоточиться на
entries.separable: inseparable — the target follows the whole phrase: home in on the problem, never ✗ home the problem in on.
entries.forms: home in on · homed in on · homed in on
entries.third person: homes in on · -ing form: homing in on
entries.transitivity: transitive — always with in on before the target

entries.meaning: To connect a machine to power, to a network, or to another machine. ---
examples: Can you hook up the speakers?
He hooked the trailer lights up in five minutes.
They're hooking up the new washer tomorrow.
entries.separable: separable — hook up the speakers, hook the speakers up; with a pronoun it must split: hook it up, never ✗ hook up it.
entries.forms: hook up · hooked up · hooked up

entries.meaning: To get someone something they want, or to put them in touch with it. ---
examples: My cousin hooked me up with tickets.
The manager hooks up regulars with free refills.
He's hooking us up with a ride to the airport.
entries.русский: подгонять, подогнать (разг.: доставать, достать); выручать, выручить
entries.separable: separable — the person is the object and normally sits inside: hook me up, hook my brother up with a ticket; the thing follows with.
entries.forms: hook up · hooked up · hooked up

entries.meaning: To have a casual sexual encounter with someone, in informal American speech. ---
examples: They hooked up after the party and never spoke again.
Everyone assumes those two are hooking up.
She hooked up with someone from her chemistry class.
entries.русский: мутить, замутить (разг.); вступать в случайную связь
entries.separable: n/a — intransitive; the other person follows with: hooked up with someone from work.
entries.forms: hook up · hooked up · hooked up

entries.meaning: To meet someone informally, usually by arrangement. ---
examples: Let's hook up after the game.
We hooked up with the others at the trailhead.
I'm hooking up with my cousins in Denver.
entries.separable: n/a — intransitive; the other person follows with: hook up with Dan after work.
entries.forms: hook up · hooked up · hooked up

entries.meaning: To play roughly or fool around instead of being serious. ---
examples: Quit horsing around — dinner's ready.
The boys horsed around in the pool all afternoon.
He horses around in class and then wonders why his grades slip.
entries.separable: n/a — intransitive; it takes no object at all.
entries.forms: horse around · horsed around · horsed around

entries.meaning: To gather closely together, for warmth or for a quick private talk. ---
examples: The team huddled up before the last play.
We huddle up for five minutes every morning.
They were huddling up under one blanket.
entries.русский: сбиваться в кучу, сбиться в кучу; собираться в кружок, собраться
entries.separable: n/a — intransitive; people huddle up, and no object can come between the parts.
entries.forms: huddle up · huddled up · huddled up

entries.meaning: To settle into one place and stay there through something difficult. ---
examples: Residents hunkered down as the hurricane came ashore.
We're hunkering down for a long negotiation.
She hunkers down in the library every finals week.
entries.separable: n/a — intransitive; no object can come between the parts.
entries.forms: hunker down · hunkered down · hunkered down

entries.meaning: To search for someone or something persistently until you find them. ---
examples: It took a week to hunt down the receipt.
Police hunted down the driver in two days.
She has been hunting down a replacement part for months.
entries.separable: separable — hunt down the suspect, hunt the suspect down; with a pronoun it must split: hunt them down.
entries.forms: hunt down · hunted down · hunted down

entries.meaning: To move or act faster, or to make someone else do so. ---
examples: Hurry up — the movie starts in ten minutes.
She hurried the kids up and out the door.
He's hurrying up to catch the last bus.
entries.separable: separable when there is an object — hurry the kids up, hurry up the order; with a pronoun it must split: hurry him up. Most often there is no object at all: hurry up, we're late.
entries.forms: hurry up · hurried up · hurried up
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (hurry up!), transitive (hurry the kids up)

entries.meaning: To keep something embarrassing secret by stopping people from talking about it. ---
examples: The district tried to hush up the report.
They hushed the whole thing up for a decade.
Nothing gets hushed up in a town this size.
entries.separable: separable — hush up the scandal, hush the story up; with a pronoun it must split: hush it up.
entries.forms: hush up · hushed up · hushed up

entries.meaning: To make someone excited and full of nervous energy. ---
examples: The DJ hyped up the crowd before the main act.
He hypes himself up with the same playlist before every game.
The kids were all hyped up on sugar by four o'clock.
entries.separable: separable — hype up the crowd, hype the crowd up; with a pronoun it must split: hype them up. Common as an adjective: the kids are all hyped up.
entries.forms: hype up · hyped up · hyped up

entries.meaning: To promote something loudly, making it sound better than it is. ---
examples: The studio hyped up the sequel for a year.
Don't hype it up too much or people will be disappointed.
Everyone's hyping up the new phone.
entries.separable: separable — hype up the movie, hype the movie up; with a pronoun it must split: hype it up.
entries.forms: hype up · hyped up · hyped up

entries.meaning: To become covered with a layer of ice. ---
examples: The pond iced over during the cold snap.
Our windshield ices over almost every night in January.
By morning the steps had iced over and nobody could get down them.
entries.separable: no object — ice over is intransitive, and the surface is the subject: the pond iced over. ✗ iced over the pond.
entries.forms: ice over · iced over · iced over

entries.meaning: To get clogged or coated with ice so that something stops working. ---
examples: The wings iced up on the way over the mountains.
If the gutters ice up, the water backs into the roof.
The lock had iced up and the key would not turn.
entries.separable: no object — ice up is intransitive: the lock iced up, never ✗ the cold iced up the lock.
entries.forms: ice up · iced up · iced up

entries.meaning: To connect one thing with another in your mind, or to be publicly connected with something. ---
examples: Most Americans identify that accent with the South.
He has been identified with the reform movement for years.
Don't identify the brand too closely with one celebrity.
entries.separable: the object comes before with: identify the smell with childhood, identify it with childhood. With still keeps its own object: ✗ identify the smell childhood with.
entries.forms: identify with · identified with · identified with

entries.meaning: To feel that you understand and share another person's feelings or situation. ---
examples: I really identified with the older sister in the movie.
Kids identify with characters their own age.
She says she has never been able to identify with her father.
entries.separable: inseparable — with never lets go of its object: I identify with her, I identify with them, never ✗ I identify her with.
entries.forms: identify with · identified with · identified with

entries.meaning: To spend time doing nothing in particular, in a way that wastes it. ---
examples: We idled away the whole afternoon on the porch.
He idles away his mornings watching the river.
I have idled half the summer away and have nothing to show for it.
entries.separable: separable — idle away the afternoon, and idle the afternoon away. With a pronoun the split is required: idled it away, never ✗ idled away it.
entries.forms: idle away · idled away · idled away

entries.meaning: To make someone understand clearly how important something is. ---
examples: My mother impressed on us that we should always call.
The coach impresses the rules on every new player.
He had impressed on her how little time was left.
entries.separable: inseparable — the person follows on: impressed on the kids, never ✗ impressed the kids on. What you want understood goes in front of on or in a how / that clause. Impress upon is the formal variant.
entries.forms: impress on · impressed on · impressed on

entries.meaning: To do or make something better than what came before. ---
examples: Nobody has improved on that record in twenty years.
The new version improves on the old one in every way.
She keeps improving on her own best time.
entries.separable: inseparable — the object stays after on: improve on her time, improve on it, never ✗ improve it on. Improve upon is the formal variant.
entries.forms: improve on · improved on · improved on

entries.meaning: To move forward very slowly, a little at a time. ---
examples: Traffic inched along for an hour.
The line inches along about one person a minute.
We were inching along in second gear the whole way.
entries.separable: no object — inch along is intransitive: traffic inched along. ✗ inched the car along.
entries.forms: inch along · inched along · inched along

entries.meaning: To rise slowly, by small amounts. ---
examples: Gas prices inched up again last week.
Her temperature has been inching up all night.
Support for the measure inches up every time somebody explains it.
entries.separable: no object — the thing that rises is the subject: prices inched up, never ✗ they inched up prices.
entries.forms: inch up · inched up · inched up

entries.meaning: To let yourself have or do something enjoyable that you usually hold back from. ---
examples: Once a week we indulge in takeout.
He indulged in a second piece of cake.
She has been indulging in long baths since the baby started sleeping.
entries.русский: позволять себе, позволить себе; предаваться, предаться
entries.separable: inseparable — what you allow yourself follows in: indulge in dessert, indulge in it, never ✗ indulge it in.
entries.forms: indulge in · indulged in · indulged in

entries.meaning: To tell the police or an authority about something someone has done wrong. ---
examples: He informed on his own partner to get a lighter sentence.
Two employees have informed on the manager.
Nobody in the neighborhood was informing on anybody.
entries.separable: inseparable — the person you report follows on: inform on his partner, inform on him, never ✗ inform him on.
entries.forms: inform on · informed on · informed on

entries.meaning: To investigate something officially in order to find out the facts. ---
examples: A committee is inquiring into the delays.
The state inquired into how the money was spent.
Two agencies have inquired into the same contract.
entries.separable: inseparable — into holds its object: inquire into the delay, inquire into it, never ✗ inquire it into.
entries.forms: inquire into · inquired into · inquired into

entries.meaning: To interrupt or disturb someone's private time or space when you are not wanted. ---
examples: I don't want to intrude on your evening.
Reporters intruded on the family for weeks.
Work keeps intruding on what is left of the weekend.
entries.separable: inseparable — on keeps its object: intrude on their evening, intrude on them, never ✗ intrude them on. Intrude upon is the formal variant.
entries.forms: intrude on · intruded on · intruded on

entries.meaning: To ask someone to come with you to something you are already going to. ---
examples: Can I invite my brother along?
They invited us along to the game.
She is inviting a few people along for the drive.
entries.русский: звать с собой, позвать с собой
entries.separable: separable — invite your brother along, and with a pronoun the object must sit in the middle: invite him along, never ✗ invite along him.
entries.forms: invite along · invited along · invited along

entries.meaning: To ask someone standing outside to come into your home or office. ---
examples: She opened the door and invited us in.
He invites the mail carrier in for coffee every winter.
They were invited in and given a seat by the fire.
entries.separable: separable — invited the neighbors in or invited in the neighbors, but a pronoun must split the pair: invited us in, never ✗ invited in us.
entries.forms: invite in · invited in · invited in

entries.meaning: To ask someone to go somewhere with you, especially on a date. ---
examples: He finally invited her out.
I am inviting the whole team out for pizza.
She has been invited out twice this week.
entries.separable: separable — invite out the whole team, invite the whole team out, and with a pronoun always invite her out, never ✗ invite out her.
entries.forms: invite out · invited out · invited out

entries.meaning: To ask someone to come to your home. ---
examples: Let's invite the Nelsons over on Saturday.
They invited us over for dinner twice last month.
She is inviting a few friends over to watch the game.
entries.русский: приглашать в гости, пригласить в гости
entries.separable: separable — invite the Nelsons over or invite over the Nelsons, and with a pronoun always invite them over, never ✗ invite over them.
entries.forms: invite over · invited over · invited over

entries.meaning: To settle the small problems or disagreements that are left in something. ---
examples: The lawyers still have to iron out a few details.
We ironed out our differences over lunch.
Once the schedule is ironed out, I will send it around.
entries.separable: separable — iron out the details, iron the details out, and with a pronoun always iron them out, never ✗ iron out them.
entries.forms: iron out · ironed out · ironed out

entries.meaning: To want something very badly and be impatient to get it. ---
examples: He has been itching for a fight all week.
By August the whole town itches for one cool morning.
The team itched for a rematch all season.
entries.separable: inseparable — what you want follows for: itching for a fight, itching for it, never ✗ itch it for. Usually in the -ing form.
entries.forms: itch for · itched for · itched for

entries.meaning: To raise a price, rate, or amount sharply; informal. ---
examples: The hotels jack up their rates during the festival.
They jacked the rent up two hundred dollars.
Premiums are being jacked up again this year.
entries.separable: separable — jack up the price, jack the price up, and with a pronoun always jack it up, never ✗ jack up it.
entries.forms: jack up · jacked up · jacked up

entries.meaning: To become blocked or stuck, or to make something blocked or stuck. ---
examples: The freeway jams up every day at five.
A wet sheet of paper jammed up the printer.
Downtown has been jamming up since the bridge closed.
entries.separable: separable when it takes an object — jammed up the printer, jammed the printer up, jammed it up — but just as often there is no object at all: the freeway jams up.
entries.forms: jam up · jammed up · jammed up
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (a wet sheet jammed up the printer), intransitive (the freeway jams up at five)

entries.meaning: To make something more lively, colorful, or interesting; informal. ---
examples: A few photos would jazz up the report.
She jazzed the plain cake up with berries.
They are jazzing up the lobby before the opening.
entries.separable: separable — jazz up the report, jazz the report up, and with a pronoun always jazz it up, never ✗ jazz up it.
entries.forms: jazz up · jazzed up · jazzed up

entries.meaning: To waste someone's time or treat them unfairly by not being straight with them; informal. ---
examples: The airline jerked us around for three days.
Stop jerking me around and tell me the price.
He felt he had been jerked around by the whole department.
entries.separable: separable, and the object almost always sits in the middle: jerk me around, jerking the customers around. ✗ jerk around me.
entries.forms: jerk around · jerked around · jerked around

entries.meaning: To agree with or match other information; American, and often spelled jive with in casual writing. ---
examples: His account doesn't jibe with the security footage.
Her numbers jibed with mine exactly.
Nothing he said was jibing with what we had been told.
entries.separable: inseparable — with keeps its object: jibe with the facts, jibe with them, never ✗ jibe them with.
entries.forms: jibe with · jibed with · jibed with

entries.meaning: To start taking part in an activity that other people have already started. ---
examples: By the second verse everybody had joined in.
She joins in every discussion.
The kids were shy at first, but they are joining in now.
entries.separable: usually no object at all — everybody joined in. When the activity is named, in holds it and cannot be split: join in the song, never ✗ join the song in.
entries.forms: join in · joined in · joined in
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (we all joined in), transitive with in (she joined in the conversation)

entries.meaning: To enlist in the armed forces. ---
examples: His grandfather joined up at eighteen.
Two of my cousins are joining up in the fall.
Plenty of people join up for the training alone.
entries.русский: вступать в армию, вступить в армию
entries.separable: no object — join up is intransitive: he joined up at eighteen. ✗ joined up the army.
entries.forms: join up · joined up · joined up

entries.meaning: To meet other people and go on together, or to team up with them. ---
examples: We will join up with the others at the trailhead.
Two small firms joined up with a national chain.
She is joining up with her sister in Denver.
entries.separable: inseparable — the three words stay together and the other party follows with: join up with them, never ✗ join them up with.
entries.forms: join up with · joined up with · joined up with
entries.third person: joins up with · -ing form: joining up with

entries.meaning: To behave in a silly, playful way, saying things you do not mean seriously. ---
examples: The two of them joke around all through practice.
We were just joking around — nobody meant it.
He has joked around so much that nobody takes his warnings seriously.
entries.separable: no object at all — joke around is intransitive: they were joking around. ✗ joke him around.
entries.forms: joke around · joked around · joked around

entries.meaning: To write something down quickly and informally, so you do not forget it. ---
examples: Let me jot down your number.
She jotted the address down on a napkin.
I have been jotting down ideas all week.
entries.separable: separable — jot down the address, jot the address down, and with a pronoun always jot it down, never ✗ jot down it.
entries.forms: jot down · jotted down · jotted down

entries.meaning: To make something more powerful or more exciting; informal. ---
examples: The new coach has juiced up the offense.
Producers juiced the trailer up with extra explosions.
They are juicing up the engine for the race.
entries.separable: separable — juice up the engine, juice the engine up, and with a pronoun always juice it up, never ✗ juice up it.
entries.forms: juice up · juiced up · juiced up

entries.meaning: To mix things together into a disordered mess. ---
examples: The move jumbled up all our boxes.
Somebody had jumbled the files up.
Stop jumbling up the dates — I cannot follow you.
entries.separable: separable — jumble up the letters, jumble the letters up, jumble them up. Most often heard in the passive: everything got jumbled up.
entries.forms: jumble up · jumbled up · jumbled up

entries.meaning: To accept an offer or a chance eagerly and without hesitating. ---
examples: She jumped at the chance to go to Tokyo.
Most students jump at free food.
I would have jumped at an offer like that.
entries.separable: inseparable — at keeps its object: jump at the chance, jump at it, never ✗ jump it at.
entries.forms: jump at · jumped at · jumped at

entries.meaning: To join a conversation or an activity suddenly, without waiting to be asked. ---
examples: Feel free to jump in if I get something wrong.
She jumped in before he could finish the sentence.
Two other people were jumping in with questions.
entries.separable: no object — jump in is intransitive: feel free to jump in. What you jump into needs into: jumped into the argument.
entries.forms: jump in · jumped in · jumped in

entries.meaning: To act on an opportunity immediately, before it is gone. ---
examples: Good apartments go fast, so jump on it.
They jumped on the discount the minute it appeared.
Every studio is jumping on the new format.
entries.русский: не упускать, не упустить (возможность); быстро хвататься
entries.separable: inseparable — what you act on follows on: jump on the offer, jump on it, never ✗ jump it on.
entries.forms: jump on · jumped on · jumped on

entries.meaning: To criticize or attack someone quickly and harshly for something they said or did. ---
examples: Don't jump on me — I am only asking.
The press jumped on one line in the speech.
He gets jumped on every time he raises the subject.
entries.separable: inseparable — the person criticized follows on: jumped on him, never ✗ jumped him on.
entries.forms: jump on · jumped on · jumped on

entries.meaning: To be so noticeable that someone sees it right away. ---
examples: One number jumped out at me right away.
Nothing in the report jumps out at you as wrong.
The typo in the headline was jumping out at everyone.
entries.русский: бросаться в глаза, броситься в глаза
entries.separable: inseparable — the three words stay in order and the person follows at: jumped out at me, never ✗ jumped me out at.
entries.forms: jump out at · jumped out at · jumped out at
entries.third person: jumps out at · -ing form: jumping out at

entries.meaning: To fall over suddenly from illness, heat, or exhaustion. ---
examples: A runner keeled over at mile twenty.
He looked like he was about to keel over.
Two people have keeled over in this heat already.
entries.русский: падать в обморок, упасть в обморок; валиться с ног, свалиться
entries.separable: n/a — no object; the particle sits right after the verb.
entries.forms: keel over · keeled over · keeled over

entries.meaning: To type numbers or information into a keypad or a computer. ---
examples: Key in your four-digit code and press the pound key.
She keyed in the wrong apartment number twice.
He's keying in the last of the invoices now.
entries.separable: separable — key in the code, and key it in; with a pronoun it must split: key it in, never ✗ key in it.
entries.forms: key in · keyed in · keyed in

entries.meaning: To discuss an idea casually, without deciding anything yet. ---
examples: We kicked around a few names for the podcast.
They've been kicking the idea around since March.
Let's kick it around at lunch and see what people think.
entries.separable: separable — kick around a few ideas, and kick them around; with a pronoun it must split: kick it around, never ✗ kick around it.
entries.forms: kick around · kicked around · kicked around

entries.meaning: To relax completely and do nothing in particular. ---
examples: We kicked back on the porch with a couple of beers.
I just want to kick back this weekend.
He's kicking back in front of the TV with the game on.
entries.separable: n/a — no object; the particle sits right after the verb.
entries.forms: kick back · kicked back · kicked back

entries.meaning: To begin to take effect or start working. ---
examples: The painkillers kicked in after about twenty minutes.
Wait in the car until the heat kicks in.
The new rules are kicking in on January first.
entries.русский: начинать действовать, начать действовать; включаться, включиться
entries.separable: n/a in this sense — no object; the medicine or the rule is the subject.
entries.forms: kick in · kicked in · kicked in

entries.meaning: To contribute money or effort to something shared. ---
examples: Everyone kicked in twenty dollars for the gift.
His parents kicked in the rest of the tuition.
If you're kicking in, tell Maria by Friday.
entries.separable: separable — kick in twenty dollars, and kick it in; it also stands alone: everybody kicked in.
entries.forms: kick in · kicked in · kicked in
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she kicked in fifty bucks), intransitive (we all kicked in)

entries.meaning: To start something, especially an event or a season. ---
examples: The mayor kicked off the campaign with a speech downtown.
The game kicks off at seven.
We're kicking off the year with a company breakfast.
entries.separable: separable — kick off the campaign, and kick it off; intransitive when the event itself begins: the game kicks off at noon.
entries.forms: kick off · kicked off · kicked off
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they kicked off the season with a parade), intransitive (the game kicks off at seven)

entries.meaning: To force someone to leave a place, a school, or a group. ---
examples: The bar kicked out two guys who were fighting.
He got kicked out of school for cheating.
They're kicking her out of the apartment at the end of the month.
entries.separable: separable — kick out the troublemakers, and kick them out; with a pronoun it must split: kick him out, never ✗ kick out him.
entries.forms: kick out · kicked out · kicked out

entries.meaning: To joke and fool around instead of being serious. ---
examples: We were just kidding around — nobody meant it.
He kids around a lot, but he does good work.
They kidded around through the whole rehearsal.
entries.separable: n/a — no object; the person you joke with follows with with: kid around with the new guy.
entries.forms: kid around · kidded around · kidded around

entries.meaning: To flatter someone in authority in order to get something from them. ---
examples: He's been kissing up to the boss all quarter.
She kissed up to the coach and still didn't start.
Don't kiss up to them — just do the work.
entries.separable: inseparable — the person always follows the whole phrase: kiss up to the boss, kiss up to her, never ✗ kiss her up to.
entries.forms: kiss up to · kissed up to · kissed up to
entries.third person: kisses up to · -ing form: kissing up to

entries.meaning: To deliberately destroy a building or a wall. ---
examples: They knocked down the old motel last spring.
We're knocking the wall down to open up the kitchen.
Half the block has been knocked down for the new stadium.
entries.separable: separable — knock down the wall, and knock it down; with a pronoun it must split: knock it down, never ✗ knock down it.
entries.forms: knock down · knocked down · knocked down

entries.meaning: To stop doing something annoying — nearly always heard as knock it off. ---
examples: Knock it off, you two — I'm on the phone.
He wouldn't knock it off until the teacher came over.
They finally knocked it off when the neighbor complained.
entries.русский: прекращать, прекратить; переставать, перестать (делать что-то раздражающее)
entries.separable: separable, and in this sense the object is almost always it — knock it off, never ✗ knock off it.
entries.forms: knock off · knocked off · knocked off

entries.meaning: To stop working for the day. ---
examples: We usually knock off around five.
They knocked off early on Friday.
I'm knocking off — see you tomorrow.
entries.русский: заканчивать работу, закончить работу; сваливать, свалить (с работы)
entries.separable: n/a in this sense — no object; a time often follows: knock off at five.
entries.forms: knock off · knocked off · knocked off

entries.meaning: To subtract an amount from a price or a total. ---
examples: The dealer knocked off five hundred dollars.
They knocked ten percent off for paying cash.
He's knocking a few dollars off because the box is damaged.
entries.separable: separable — knock off twenty dollars, and knock twenty dollars off; the amount can sit on either side.
entries.forms: knock off · knocked off · knocked off

entries.meaning: To beat a team or a player so that they leave a competition. ---
examples: Spain knocked us out in the quarterfinals.
The defending champion was knocked out in the first round.
One more loss knocks them out of the playoffs.
entries.separable: separable — knock out the favorites, and knock them out; the losing team can also sit inside: knocked us out.
entries.forms: knock out · knocked out · knocked out

entries.meaning: To damage something so badly that it stops working. ---
examples: The storm knocked out power to forty thousand homes.
A single lightning strike can knock the servers out.
Cell service has been knocked out since Tuesday.
entries.русский: выводить из строя, вывести из строя; отключать, отключить
entries.separable: separable — knock out the power, and knock it out.
entries.forms: knock out · knocked out · knocked out

entries.meaning: To hit someone hard enough to make them lose consciousness. ---
examples: He knocked out his opponent in the second round.
That medicine knocks me out for ten hours.
She was knocked out cold when the branch came down.
entries.separable: separable — knock out the champion, and knock him out; with a pronoun it must split: knock me out, never ✗ knock out me.
entries.forms: knock out · knocked out · knocked out

entries.meaning: To produce or finish something quickly, without much fuss. ---
examples: I'll knock out the slides tonight.
She knocked three chapters out over the weekend.
He's been knocking out two of these a day.
entries.русский: делать быстро, сделать быстро; строчить, настрочить
entries.separable: separable — knock out a draft, and knock it out.
entries.forms: knock out · knocked out · knocked out

entries.meaning: To start working hard and seriously at something. ---
examples: You'll have to knuckle down if you want to pass.
He finally knuckled down two weeks before the exam.
She's knuckling down on the thesis this month.
entries.русский: браться за дело, взяться за дело; приниматься за работу, приняться за работу
entries.separable: n/a — no object; the work follows with to: knuckle down to the reading.
entries.forms: knuckle down · knuckled down · knuckled down

entries.meaning: To develop or move more slowly than others and fall back. ---
examples: Wages have lagged behind inflation for years.
He lagged behind the rest of the group on the climb.
Our region is lagging behind on broadband.
entries.separable: inseparable — what you trail follows the whole phrase: lag behind the competition, lag behind them, never ✗ lag them behind.
entries.forms: lag behind · lagged behind · lagged behind
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wages lagged behind inflation), intransitive (sales are lagging behind)

entries.meaning: To enjoy praise or attention greedily, or to accept something without questioning it. ---
examples: He lapped up the applause.
The crowd is lapping it up.
They lapped up every word of his story.
entries.separable: separable — lap up the attention, and lap it up; with a pronoun it must split: lap it up, never ✗ lap up it.
entries.forms: lap up · lapped up · lapped up

entries.meaning: To suddenly attack someone with angry words. ---
examples: He lashed out at the reporters on the courthouse steps.
She lashes out when she's tired.
They've been lashing out at each other all week.
entries.русский: срываться, сорваться (на ком-то); набрасываться, наброситься (с упрёками)
entries.separable: n/a — no object; the target follows with at: lash out at reporters.
entries.forms: lash out · lashed out · lashed out

entries.meaning: To seize on an idea or attach yourself to a person and not let go. ---
examples: The press latched onto one line of the speech.
He latched onto us at the party and stayed all night.
Kids latch onto whatever their friends are doing.
entries.русский: цепляться, уцепиться (за что-то); привязываться, привязаться (к кому-то)
entries.separable: inseparable — latch onto an idea, latch onto him, never ✗ latch him onto.
entries.forms: latch onto · latched onto · latched onto

entries.meaning: To treat something serious as a joke so that it seems unimportant. ---
examples: He laughed off the rumor at the press conference.
She laughed it off, but it clearly stung.
They're laughing off the criticism for now.
entries.separable: separable — laugh off the question, and laugh it off; with a pronoun it must split: laugh it off, never ✗ laugh off it.
entries.forms: laugh off · laughed off · laughed off

entries.meaning: To start doing or saying something energetically and at length. ---
examples: He launched into a twenty-minute story about his car.
She launches into the same complaint every time.
The band launched into the chorus before the crowd sat down.
entries.русский: пускаться, пуститься (в рассказ, в спор); начинать с жаром, начать
entries.separable: inseparable — launch into a speech, launch into it, never ✗ launch it into.
entries.forms: launch into · launched into · launched into

entries.meaning: To turn the pages of something quickly without reading it carefully. ---
examples: She leafed through the magazine in the waiting room.
He's leafing through the file now.
I leaf through the catalog every time it comes.
entries.separable: inseparable — leaf through a magazine, leaf through it, never ✗ leaf it through.
entries.forms: leaf through · leafed through · leafed through

entries.meaning: To become known when it was meant to stay secret. ---
examples: The memo leaked out two days before the announcement.
Details are leaking out now.
If this leaks out, we're finished.
entries.separable: n/a — no object; the information is the subject: the memo leaked out.
entries.forms: leak out · leaked out · leaked out

entries.meaning: To stop rising or falling and stay steady. ---
examples: Prices leveled off in the spring.
The plane levels off at thirty thousand feet.
Enrollment is leveling off after five years of growth.
entries.separable: n/a — no object; the thing that steadies is the subject.
entries.forms: level off · leveled off · leveled off

entries.meaning: To tell someone the honest truth, even when it is unwelcome. ---
